description: AI-generated interview questions, flashcards, and guided challenges for DBMS, OS, Networking, and System Design — the four pillars of the Core CS section in CodeConfidence.

questions.front: What is a Transaction? What are its states?
questions.back:
A transaction is a sequence of database operations treated as a single logical unit. Transaction states:
1. Active: Operations being executed
2. Partially Committed: Last operation executed, awaiting confirmation
3. Committed: All operations complete successfully, changes permanent
4. Failed: An error occurred, normal execution can't proceed
5. Aborted: Rolled back to previous state
6. Terminated: Transaction ended (committed or aborted)
questions.pseudocode:
BEGIN TRANSACTION
    → State: Active
    READ(A), WRITE(B)
    → State: Partially Committed
    IF success:
        COMMIT → State: Committed (permanent)
    ELSE:
        ROLLBACK → State: Aborted (changes undone)
END TRANSACTION → State: Terminated

questions.front: What are the different types of database keys?
questions.back:
• Super Key: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row
• Candidate Key: Minimal super key (no redundant attributes)
• Primary Key: Chosen candidate key — unique + not null
• Alternate Key: Candidate keys not chosen as primary key
• Foreign Key: Attribute referencing the primary key of another table
• Composite Key: A key made of multiple attributes
• Surrogate Key: Artificial key (auto-increment ID) with no business meaning
questions.example:
Table: Employee(EmpID, Email, SSN, Name)
• Super Keys: {EmpID}, {Email}, {SSN}, {EmpID, Email}, ...
• Candidate Keys: {EmpID}, {Email}, {SSN} (all minimal)
• Primary Key: EmpID (chosen)
• Alternate Keys: Email, SSN

questions.question: Explain the difference between clustered and non-clustered indexes.
questions.model_answer: A clustered index determines the physical order of data in the table — the data rows are stored in the order of the clustered index key. There can be only ONE clustered index per table (usually the primary key). A non-clustered index is a separate structure that stores the index key and a pointer to the actual data row. Multiple non-clustered indexes can exist. Clustered indexes are faster for range queries; non-clustered are better for selective lookups on non-primary columns.

questions.question: What is a deadlock in DBMS? How is it different from a livelock?
questions.model_answer: A DBMS deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are permanently waiting for each other to release locks — none can proceed. A livelock is when transactions keep changing state in response to each other but never make progress (they're active but stuck in a loop). Deadlock prevention techniques: lock ordering, timeout-based rollback, wound-wait, wait-die protocols.

questions.front: What is the difference between TRUNCATE, DELETE, and DROP?
questions.back:
• DELETE: DML command. Removes specific rows (WHERE clause). Logged (can rollback). Triggers fire. Slower.
• TRUNCATE: DDL command. Removes ALL rows. Not logged per-row (faster). Cannot rollback in most DBs. Resets AUTO_INCREMENT. No triggers.
• DROP: DDL command. Removes the entire table (structure + data). Cannot rollback. Frees storage.
questions.example:
DELETE FROM Students WHERE gpa < 5;  -- removes specific rows
TRUNCATE TABLE Students;              -- removes all rows, keeps structure
DROP TABLE Students;                  -- removes table entirely

questions.front: What is thrashing in an OS?
questions.back: Thrashing occurs when a system spends more time swapping pages in and out of memory (paging) than executing actual processes. It happens when there are too many processes competing for limited physical memory, causing constant page faults. Resolution: Reduce degree of multiprogramming, use working set model, increase RAM.

questions.question: Explain the difference between internal and external fragmentation.
questions.model_answer: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated memory is larger than what is actually needed — the extra space inside the allocated block is wasted. It happens with fixed-size memory allocation (e.g., paging). External fragmentation occurs when there is enough total free memory but it's scattered in non-contiguous blocks — no single large enough block exists. It happens with variable-size allocation (e.g., segmentation). Paging eliminates external fragmentation but causes internal. Segmentation eliminates internal but causes external.
ai_hints: Did you explain both types clearly?
Did you mention which allocation method causes which type?
Did you mention paging and segmentation?

questions.front: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
questions.back: Preemptive: CPU can be taken away from a process before it finishes (e.g., Round Robin, SRTF, Priority with preemption). Non-preemptive: Once a process gets CPU, it runs until it completes or blocks voluntarily (e.g., FCFS, SJF without preemption). Preemptive is better for responsiveness (used in modern OSes). Non-preemptive is simpler but can cause starvation and convoy effect.

questions.question: What are the different states of a process? Draw the process state diagram.
questions.model_answer: A process goes through 5 states: New (process being created), Ready (in RAM, waiting for CPU), Running (being executed on CPU), Waiting/Blocked (waiting for I/O or event), Terminated (finished execution). Transitions: New→Ready (admitted), Ready→Running (CPU scheduled), Running→Ready (preempted/time quantum expired), Running→Waiting (I/O request), Waiting→Ready (I/O complete), Running→Terminated (exit).

questions.front: What are the different types of OS kernel architectures?
questions.back:
• Monolithic Kernel: All OS services (memory, process, device drivers) run in kernel space. Fast but complex and less fault-tolerant. (Linux, Unix)
• Microkernel: Only core services (IPC, basic scheduling, memory) in kernel. Rest run in user space. More stable but slower due to IPC overhead. (QNX, Mach)
• Hybrid Kernel: Combination of monolithic and microkernel. (Windows NT, macOS XNU)
• Exokernel: Minimal kernel — exposes hardware directly to user programs. Max flexibility, max complexity.

questions.front: What is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) and how does it work?
questions.back: ARP resolves a known IP address to an unknown MAC address on the same local network. Devices need the MAC address to send Ethernet frames but only know the IP address. ARP sends a broadcast asking 'Who has IP 192.168.1.5?'. The device with that IP replies with its MAC address. The result is cached in the ARP table.
questions.pseudocode:
// ARP Process
Device A wants to send to 192.168.1.5

Step 1: Check ARP cache
  ARP Table: { 192.168.1.1 → AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:01 }
  192.168.1.5 → NOT FOUND

Step 2: Broadcast ARP Request
  From: A (192.168.1.1, MAC: AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:01)
  To: BROADCAST (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF)
  Ask: 'Who has 192.168.1.5? Tell 192.168.1.1'

Step 3: Device B (192.168.1.5) replies
  ARP Reply (unicast): '192.168.1.5 is at AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:05'

Step 4: Device A caches the result
  ARP Table updated: { 192.168.1.5 → AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:05 }

Step 5: Send actual data using the MAC address

questions.question: What is DNS? Explain the full DNS resolution process.
questions.model_answer: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (www.google.com) to IP addresses. DNS resolution: Browser checks local cache → OS cache → /etc/hosts → Recursive Resolver → Root Nameserver (returns .com TLD nameserver) → TLD Nameserver (returns google.com authoritative nameserver) → Authoritative Nameserver (returns actual IP) → IP returned to browser and cached.
questions.pseudocode:
// DNS Resolution for www.google.com

1. Browser cache: 'google.com → ?' — MISS
2. OS resolver cache — MISS
3. /etc/hosts file — MISS
4. Query Recursive Resolver (ISP's or 8.8.8.8)

5. Recursive Resolver asks Root Nameserver:
   'Who handles .com?'
   Root → 'Ask a.gtld-servers.net (TLD for .com)'

6. Recursive Resolver asks .com TLD Nameserver:
   'Who handles google.com?'
   TLD → 'Ask ns1.google.com (Authoritative NS)'

7. Recursive Resolver asks google.com Authoritative NS:
   'What is the IP for www.google.com?'
   Authoritative → '142.250.190.46' (A record)

8. Recursive Resolver returns IP to browser
   Browser caches: www.google.com → 142.250.190.46 (TTL: 300s)

9. Browser connects to 142.250.190.46
ai_hints: Did you explain all 4 actors: Browser, Recursive Resolver, Root NS, Authoritative NS?
Did you mention DNS caching and TTL?
Did you mention the A record?

questions.back: NAT allows multiple devices on a private network to share a single public IP address. The router maintains a NAT table mapping private IP:port combinations to public IP:port. This conserves IPv4 addresses and adds a layer of security (internal devices are hidden). Types: Static NAT (1:1 mapping), Dynamic NAT (pool of public IPs), PAT/Masquerade (many:1 using different ports — most common in home routers).

questions.question: What is the difference between a hub, switch, and router?
questions.model_answer: Hub (Layer 1): Broadcasts all incoming data to all ports regardless of destination. Causes collisions, inefficient. Switch (Layer 2): Sends data only to the specific port where the destination MAC address is connected. Maintains a MAC address table. Efficient, reduces collisions. Router (Layer 3): Connects different networks and routes packets based on IP addresses using a routing table. Performs NAT, DHCP, and firewall functions in home routers.

questions.front: What are the common HTTP status codes?
questions.back:
• 1xx Informational: 100 Continue
• 2xx Success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
• 3xx Redirection: 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found (temporary), 304 Not Modified (cached)
• 4xx Client Errors: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests
• 5xx Server Errors: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout

questions.question: What is a firewall? Explain the types of firewalls.
questions.model_answer: A firewall is a network security device that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic based on security rules. Types: Packet Filter Firewall (inspects packets at network/transport layer — checks IP/port/protocol), Stateful Inspection Firewall (tracks connection state — allows only responses to established connections), Application Layer Firewall / WAF (inspects HTTP content — protects against SQL injection, XSS), Next-Gen Firewall (NGFW) (combines all of the above with deep packet inspection and threat intelligence).
questions.pseudocode:
// Packet Filter Rules Example
ALLOW TCP from ANY to 192.168.1.100 port 80   // HTTP in
ALLOW TCP from ANY to 192.168.1.100 port 443  // HTTPS in
DENY TCP from ANY to 192.168.1.100 port 22    // SSH blocked
DENY ALL                                        // default deny

// Stateful Inspection
Outbound: 192.168.1.10:5001 → 8.8.8.8:53 (DNS query) → ALLOW + track state
Inbound:  8.8.8.8:53 → 192.168.1.10:5001 (DNS reply) → ALLOW (matches state)
Inbound:  Unsolicited packet from unknown → DENY (no matching state)

// WAF (Web App Firewall)
Request: GET /users?id=1 OR 1=1  ← SQL Injection
WAF detects pattern → BLOCK + log + alert

questions.front: What is horizontal vs vertical scaling?
questions.back: Vertical Scaling (Scale Up): Add more resources (CPU, RAM) to a single server. Simpler but has a limit and single point of failure. Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out): Add more servers and distribute load. More complex but limitless and fault-tolerant. Most modern systems use horizontal scaling with a load balancer.

questions.front: What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
questions.back: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of servers (edge servers) that cache and deliver static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) to users from the nearest location, reducing latency. When a user requests content, the CDN serves from the closest edge server. If not cached (cache miss), it fetches from the origin server (cache miss → origin pull). Examples: Cloudflare, AWS CloudFront, Akamai.

questions.question: What is a message queue? When would you use Kafka vs RabbitMQ?
questions.model_answer: A message queue decouples producers (who send messages) from consumers (who process them), enabling async communication and handling load spikes. Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform — messages are stored durably, consumers can replay events, designed for very high throughput (millions of events/sec). Best for: event streaming, analytics, audit logs, microservices event bus. RabbitMQ is a traditional message broker — messages are consumed and deleted, supports complex routing with exchanges and bindings. Best for: task queues, RPC, work distribution, order processing.

questions.back:
S – Single Responsibility: A class should have only one reason to change.
O – Open/Closed: Open for extension, closed for modification.
L – Liskov Substitution: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
I – Interface Segregation: No client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use.
D – Dependency Inversion: High-level modules should not depend on low-level ones. Both should depend on abstractions.

questions.question: Design a notification system that can send notifications via Email, SMS, and Push. It should be extensible to new channels.
questions.model_answer: Use the Strategy Pattern combined with the Observer Pattern. Define a Notification interface with a send() method. Implement EmailNotification, SMSNotification, PushNotification as concrete strategies. A NotificationService accepts a list of channels and a message, then invokes each channel's send() method. Adding a new channel (e.g., WhatsApp) requires only a new class implementing the interface — no modification to existing code (Open/Closed principle).
questions.pseudocode:
// Strategy Pattern + Open/Closed
INTERFACE NotificationChannel:
    FUNCTION send(recipient, message)

CLASS EmailNotification IMPLEMENTS NotificationChannel:
    FUNCTION send(recipient, message):
        EMAIL_API.send(to=recipient.email, body=message)

CLASS SMSNotification IMPLEMENTS NotificationChannel:
    FUNCTION send(recipient, message):
        SMS_API.send(to=recipient.phone, text=message)

CLASS PushNotification IMPLEMENTS NotificationChannel:
    FUNCTION send(recipient, message):
        FCM.push(device_token=recipient.deviceToken, body=message)

CLASS NotificationService:
    channels: LIST of NotificationChannel

    FUNCTION notify(recipient, message, channelTypes):
        FOR each type in channelTypes:
            channel = channelFactory(type)  // factory returns right impl
            channel.send(recipient, message)

// Adding WhatsApp later:
CLASS WhatsAppNotification IMPLEMENTS NotificationChannel:
    FUNCTION send(recipient, message):
        WHATSAPP_API.send(recipient.phone, message)
// Zero changes to existing code!
ai_hints: Did you use an interface/abstract class?
Is adding a new channel easy without modifying existing code?
Did you mention the design patterns used?
